strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: DADO connects classical max-product message passing on junction trees with distributional optimization/EDAs, generalizing prior work that was limited to fully decomposed objectives (FDA) or chain-structured policies (coordination-graph policy optimization).

The theoretical development is careful: distributional value functions are shown to lower-bound classical value functions (Eq. 10/32), Monte Carlo estimates are unbiased, and an alternative derivation from a maximum-entropy objective (Sec. A.4) lends credibility and generality to the framework.

The empirical evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: multiple synthetic problem sizes (L=25, 50, 100/200), seven protein property predictors from real datasets, ablations over sample budget K, per-method hyperparameter sweeps with checks that optima are not on sweep boundaries, 20 seeds, and paired statistical tests on AUC.

The case study on decomposition threshold (Fig. A5) thoughtfully addresses the practical trade-off between predictive accuracy and decomposability, and the discussion of limitations (e.g., intrinsically disordered proteins like Gcn4) is candid.
Code and dataset details are provided, supporting reproducibility; the paper is well written with good intuition-building (Fig. 1).
weaknesses: Baselines are limited to a single 'naive' EDA. The paper positions DADO against FDA (Mühlenbein & Mahnig 1999) and chain-structured policy optimization in related work, but never compares empirically to these or other strong discrete optimizers (e.g., cross-entropy method variants, MCMC-based, GFlowNets, RL approaches like PPO/TRPO adapted to decomposed objectives), making it hard to assess the practical magnitude of the contribution.

The decomposable objectives used in the protein experiments are constructed by the authors themselves (MLPs constrained to a junction tree from AlphaFold contact maps). Real-world predictive models are not naturally decomposable, so end-to-end utility for actual scientific design (e.g., quality/diversity/validity of designed sequences against ground truth or wet-lab evidence) is not demonstrated; the claimed benefit is mostly on the authors' own surrogate class.

The central claim of improved statistical efficiency is argued intuitively (larger samples-to-dimension ratio per factor) but not formalized; no sample-complexity analysis or characterization of when the decomposition must hold for gains to materialize.

No compute/cost accounting: DADO requires evaluating node/edge component functions and per-factor MLP updates each iteration; whether it is favorable under a wall-clock or FLOP-matched budget relative to the naive EDA is not reported.

Moderate novelty: the method is a fairly natural combination of known ingredients (max-product message passing, coordination graphs, weighted MLE/EDA updates), and substantial derivation material is duplicated between Sec. 2.1 and Sec. A.3.

A few experimental design choices reduce confidence, e.g., hyperparameters tuned by selecting the largest final sample mean (which may favor instability), and significance testing on AUC of mean curves across seeds assumes independence that paired curves may not fully satisfy.

strengths: The paper is clearly written, and the derivation from classical max-product message passing on junction trees to distributional value functions (Eq. 7-14) is coherent and technically plausible. The connection to distributional value functions lower-bounding classical value functions (Eq. 10, 32) is a nice touch.
The problem setting is relevant: leveraging decomposability structure in property predictors for discrete design is a genuinely under-explored angle relative to the literature on model inaccuracy.

The experimental methodology is careful in places: hyperparameter sweeps done separately per method, paired t-tests over 20 seeds, ablations on sample budget K, and a case study on decomposition strength (Fig. A5). Code is publicly released.
The related work section positions the contribution against FDA, policy optimization over chains, and high-dimensional BO reasonably well.
weaknesses: The evaluation is largely circular with respect to the central claim. In the protein experiments, the surrogate f(x) is itself constructed to adhere to the junction tree decomposition (an MLP per node/edge component). DADO is then shown to optimize this same decomposed object better than a naive EDA. This largely tests whether a decomposition-aware optimizer beats a decomposition-unaware one on a function built from the very structure it exploits — an almost foregone conclusion — rather than whether DADO yields better real-world designs. No ground-truth or in vitro validation of any designed sequences is provided.

The baseline comparison is very weak. The only competitor is a naive autoregressive EDA. No comparison to other distributional optimization or RL methods (PPO, CbAS, CMA-ES, FDA/BOA variants, or decomposition-aware policy optimization), no BO baselines, and no ablation isolating the benefit of message-passing weights versus simply having a factorized search distribution.

The key assumption — that a contact graph from an AlphaFold3 wild-type structure thresholded at 4.5Å yields a decomposition that reflects the true epistasis of the property — is unvalidated. The paper's own appendix concedes the approach fails on intrinsically disordered proteins (Gcn4, very poor holdout accuracy), and the predictors are trained mostly on double mutants, so out-of-distribution f(x) values driving the reported 'improvements' are of questionable reliability.

Results are mixed and possibly fragile: on TDP-43 (the longest protein) there is no meaningful difference at K=1000; the advantage appears mainly on shorter/saturated landscapes, and the appendix shows the advantage can flip depending on K and contact threshold. The generality of the claimed efficiency gain is thus not established.

Novelty is incremental relative to the Factorized Distribution Algorithm and coordination-graph message passing (Vlassis et al., 2004): the main step is replacing max with an expectation over the current search distribution in the messages, which is a fairly natural adaptation of standard EDA/advantage-weighted regression machinery to tree-structured objectives.

The claimed 'statistical efficiency' of per-factor updates is asserted heuristically (samples-to-dimensions ratio) but never analyzed theoretically; no sample-complexity analysis or convergence guarantees are given, despite the derivation suggesting such a result is within reach.

Scalability is unaddressed for realistic settings: all protein experiments use short segments (L=28-118) of much larger proteins (e.g., AAV full length 735), and the per-node/edge MLP factor architecture grows with junction tree complexity; the cost and practicality of the procedure at scale, or how the decomposition is chosen in general, is not seriously evaluated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core contribution: DADO extends classical max-product message-passing (exact optimization on junction trees) to distributional optimization, generalizing factorized policy optimization from Markov-chain settings to arbitrary tree decompositions. This connection is novel in the EDA/design literature and is carefully argued.

The derivation is technically careful: the distributional value functions are motivated as Monte-Carlo-tractable lower bounds of classical value functions (Eq. 10/32), the update rule is derived cleanly from the EDA/EM view, and an alternate maximum-entropy derivation (Sec. A.4) lends credibility and shows the method is one instance of a broader framework.

Experiments span synthetic landscapes with controlled difficulty (varying L, K, reciprocal-sign-epistasis) and seven real protein datasets (Amyloid, AAV, GB1, TDP-43, ynzC, CreiLOV, Gcn4), with 20 seeds, AUC-based paired t-tests, and per-method hyperparameter sweeps — a reasonably rigorous empirical protocol.

Honest reporting of negative/neutral results: TDP-43, ynzC, and CreiLOV show no advantage at K=1000, and the Gcn4 intrinsically-disordered-protein case shows the decomposition pipeline can fail; these are discussed rather than hidden.
The GB1 threshold case study (Fig. A5) usefully probes the accuracy-vs-decomposability tradeoff and shows when DADO's advantage appears and disappears.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, dataset provenance, and public code.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is thin. The only comparison is a naive, decomposition-unaware EDA. No comparison against the directly-related FDA, against strong modern baselines (e.g., PPO/TRPO-style policy optimization, CbAS, MCMC-based discrete optimizers, or BO approaches exploiting additivity such as those the authors themselves cite), or against exact message-passing when the junction tree allows it. Given that the entire claimed benefit is statistical efficiency of optimization, the evidence that DADO beats methods beyond the weakest strawman is limited.

Evaluation is entirely in silico on the surrogate f(x) that the authors themselves construct to be decomposable. There is a circularity concern: DADO's advantage on proteins partly stems from choosing a restrictive model class (strict junction-tree factorization, e.g., t=2.75Å) that happens to be easier for DADO to optimize, rather than from demonstrating better designs under a fixed, realistic objective. No wet-lab or independent-oracle validation of the designs is provided.

The headline claim of greater statistical efficiency is asserted via intuition (sample-to-dimension ratio) but never formalized; no theory characterizing when the lower-bound substitution or the per-factor updates preserve the DO optimum, nor convergence properties. The correctness of the coupled update relies on Q-functions being 'valid while θ is close to θ^n,' which is hand-waved.

Several practical settings show little or no benefit: at K=1000, three of seven protein problems show no significant difference, and the advantage on proteins materializes mainly at smaller K or under stricter decompositions. The practical scope of the win is narrower than the abstract suggests.

The method requires a known or estimated decomposition, and the predictive model must be retrained to conform to that decomposition, potentially sacrificing accuracy (only briefly quantified on GB1). The cost and difficulty of obtaining good decompositions outside proteins (circuit, telescope examples are hypothetical only) is unaddressed empirically.

Comparison is on model-based score curves only; no diversity/novelty analysis of generated designs, which matters greatly for the design use case, and no discussion of degenerate/collapsed outputs given no entropy regularization in the main algorithm.

strengths: The paper presents a clean, well-motivated contribution: generalizing max-plus message passing from exact optimization on junction trees (coordination graphs, Vlassis et al., 2004) to distributional optimization/EDAs via 'distributional value functions', yielding DADO. The derivation (Sec. 2.1, A.4) is careful, correct, and the connection between classical and distributional value functions (Eq. 19-22) is clearly explained.

The paper also provides an alternative derivation via a maximum-entropy objective (Sec. A.5), showing the method is robust to the choice of derivation and situating the contribution within a broader framework of decomposition-aware DO.

Evaluation is thorough for an algorithmic paper: synthetic experiments with exact tree decompositions across increasing L (25-400) and D (20-100), seven real protein datasets, three baselines (naive EDA, FDA which shares DADO's factorization isolating the value-function contribution, and a PPO variant), 20 random seeds with paired t-tests, hyperparameter sweeps for all methods, runtime analysis, and sensitivity studies showing the method is robust to imperfect decompositions.

The FDA baseline is well chosen: giving FDA the same factorization cleanly decomposes DADO's advantage into factorization vs. message-passing weights, and the results on GB1/ynzC/CreiLOV where FDA ties or beats DADO honestly delineate the method's scope (small junction-tree nodes).
Good reproducibility: implementation details, architectures, hyperparameter sweeps, and dataset sources are all specified; code is stated to be publicly available.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. The method is a fairly natural combination of known components: FDA-style factorized search distributions plus max-plus message-passing weights, and the maximum-entropy derivation closely follows Levine (2018). The key extension beyond coordination-graph RL (which handles chains) to general junction trees is useful but arguably incremental.

The protein experiments have a circularity concern: the 'real-data' objectives are decomposed surrogate models constructed by imposing the AlphaFold3-derived junction tree and fitting MLP component functions. No experiment evaluates the resulting designs against a truly independent oracle (e.g., a large protein language model or experimental proxy), so the practical claim of 'potential for practical utility on protein design' rests on optimizing a model that was built to respect DADO's required structure. The robustness studies (A.9.4-A.9.6) partially mitigate this but do not fully resolve it.

Baselines are limited to EDA, FDA, and a PPO variant. No comparison to modern model-based optimization or BO-with-additive-structure methods the paper itself cites (e.g., Kandasamy et al., Rolland et al., Ziomek & Ammar), nor to widely used MBO methods (CbAS, DbAS), making it hard to gauge DADO against the current state of the art.

Performance gains are setting-dependent: on 3 of 7 protein datasets (larger junction-tree nodes), DADO fails to beat FDA, and the main-text proteins were explicitly selected for favorable (small-node) decompositions. The paper discusses this honestly, but the main-text presentation somewhat oversells generality.

No convergence or optimality guarantees: only a lower-bound argument is given, and key trade-offs (gradient steps per iteration, variance of Monte-Carlo value functions as node cardinality grows) are discussed qualitatively and hypothesized about (A.9.3) but not analyzed theoretically or empirically characterized.

Synthetic functions use an exact tree decomposition (node size 1); there is no synthetic study with realistic partial/deep decompositions, which limits understanding of where the efficiency boundary lies.

strengths: The derivation of DADO is clean and well-motivated: the paper carefully connects classical max-plus message passing to a distributional optimization formulation, and the alternative maximum-entropy derivation (Sec. A.5) strengthens the conceptual contribution by showing the framework is derivable from multiple objectives.

The algorithm is properly positioned against related work, particularly FDA (Mühlenbein & Mahnig, 1999), and the FDA baseline is implemented with the same factorization as DADO, which cleanly isolates the contribution of message-passing value functions over mere search-distribution factorization.

Experiments cover synthetic problems (varying L up to 400 and D up to 100), four protein property predictors in the main text, and three more in the appendix, with 20 seeds, paired t-tests, tuned baselines, runtime analysis, and released code—above-average empirical diligence for this problem area.

The appendix studies robustness of the decomposition (contact threshold variation, random edge add/remove, bottom-50% training data), addressing the important practical question of how exact the assumed decomposition must be.
The choice of baselines (naive EDA, FDA, PPO) is reasonable for isolating the effect of decomposition-awareness within the EDA/policy-optimization family.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is somewhat circular: for the protein experiments, the authors themselves construct the decomposed property predictor from the AlphaFold3 contact graph, and then show that DADO optimizes this self-constructed decomposed objective better. The claimed practical benefit only exists for objectives that the practitioner has deliberately built to be decomposable; there is no experiment showing DADO improves optimization of standard, off-the-shelf property predictors (e.g., protein language models or non-decomposed surrogate models), which is the setting most users actually face.

No true end-to-end validation: all results are against surrogate models fit by the authors. There is no wet-lab, ground-truth, or independent-model confirmation that designs found by DADO are actually better, so the significance for scientific design remains asserted rather than demonstrated.

The method's advantages degrade precisely where it would matter most: on GB1, ynzC, and CreiLOV—proteins with larger junction-tree nodes—DADO does not beat FDA (Fig. A4), and the authors' own variance explanation suggests the Monte-Carlo value-function estimates are unreliable when decompositions are coarse. Only 4 of 7 datasets were featured in the main text, and the selection criteria (small nodes, distant-mutation data) favor DADO, raising concerns about cherry-picking.

No comparison against stronger model-based optimization baselines outside the EDA family (e.g., CbAS, additive-model BO like the methods cited in Sec. 3, diffusion-based design as in Uehara et al. 2024), despite the authors citing these as complementary; the competitive relevance of DADO beyond naive EDAs is unestablished.

The method requires a junction-tree decomposition and tractable node cardinalities; practical applicability to realistic protein design problems (long sequences, dense contact maps like CreiLOV) appears limited, and the paper offers no solution other than noting lower thresholds 'could' help without testing optimization there.

Several important design choices (mean-shifted Q-functions, shaping function temperature, number of gradient steps G=1) are justified only empirically or by appeal to standard practice; no theoretical analysis of convergence or of the gap between the optimized lower-bound objective (Eq. 5) and the true EDA objective is provided.
Writing is at times verbose and repetitive (the same intuition is re-derived across Secs. 1, 2, A.3, A.4), and the reproducibility statement references a GitHub link that appears incomplete.

strengths: The core idea is clean, well-motivated, and novel within the EDA/distributional optimization literature: exploiting junction-tree decomposability of the objective via distributional value functions and message passing to coordinate factor-wise updates of the search distribution. The distinction from FDA (factorized search distribution without value-function weighting) is clearly articulated and experimentally isolated.

The derivation is thorough and technically sound: the equivalence between classical max-plus message passing and the distributional formulation, the lower-bound argument (Eq. 23), the per-factor weighted MLE update rule, and the alternative maximum-entropy derivation (Sec. A.5) collectively give a convincing theoretical grounding and suggest a general framework rather than a one-off trick.

Experimental design is reasonably careful: hyperparameter sweeps per method per objective, 20 random seeds, paired statistical tests, a runtime analysis (Table 1), and honest reporting of cases where DADO does not win (GB1/ynzC vs. FDA in Fig. A4).

The robustness studies (contact-threshold sweeps, random graph mutations, bottom-50% training data in Sec. A.9.4–A.9.6) address the important practical question of whether an approximate decomposition suffices, and the case study on GB1 (Fig. A6) nicely illustrates the accuracy-vs-decomposability tradeoff.
The paper is well written, with good pedagogical structure (from naive EDA, to exact message passing, to the distributional generalization), and includes a reproducibility statement with public code.
weaknesses: Baseline comparisons are limited and somewhat weak. The comparisons are essentially restricted to a naive EDA, FDA, and a PPO-style variant. No comparison is made to modern model-based optimization approaches (e.g., CbAS, COMs, conservative fine-tuning of generative models cited as complementary), nor to the additively decomposed BO methods (Kandasamy et al. 2015; Rolland et al. 2018; Ziomek & Ammar 2023) that the related-work section argues are closely adjacent. This makes the practical significance of the gains hard to judge.

There is a circularity concern in the protein experiments: the authors construct the decomposed property predictor themselves (enforcing the junction-tree structure when fitting f(x)), and then evaluate methods by optimization performance on that same surrogate. DADO may benefit by construction from optimizing a function engineered to match its assumptions, and improvements in f(x) do not demonstrate improved real protein property. No external validation of designed sequences (e.g., comparison of top designs' predicted labels under an independent model, novelty/diversity analysis, or wet-lab/structure-based checks) is provided.

The synthetic experiments use an exact tree decomposition with node size one and pairwise lookup tables — the best-case scenario for DADO. Experiments where the decomposition is only approximate or the objective does not respect the assumed topology are limited to the protein case studies and are less controlled.

DADO does not consistently beat FDA on the less-decomposable proteins (GB1, ynzC; CreiLOV is worse), and the hypothesized explanation (variance in value functions for large nodes) is not tested. The method's applicability thus appears confined to problems with genuinely small junction-tree nodes, which narrows the claimed scope of 'any decomposability defined by a junction tree.'

No convergence or approximation-quality analysis is provided for the iterative algorithm: the observations that {Q_i^θ} are only valid near θ^n and that gradient-step count must be balanced are discussed informally, but there is no theory characterizing when DADO converges, how the lower bound tightens, or failure modes.

Main-text experimental scope is modest (three synthetic functions, four of seven protein datasets, with the latter chosen post hoc by decomposability criteria), which slightly weakens the generality of the empirical claims.
